figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: TimeOpt schematic. (a) The position spline and its control points $u_{i}$ remain fixed; purple markers indicate positions at path knots. (b) Optimizing coefficients $r_{i}$ changes the squared path speed $x_{r}(s)$. (c) The resulting time map assigns unequal traversal times to the same path intervals. In this example, slower traversal through the shaded region and faster traversal elsewhere reduce the total duration.
figures.headline: Retiming changes the squared path speed with the position spline fixed, so the same path intervals receive different traversal times.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: TimeOpt solver. The predictor and corrector reuse one Cholesky factorization. In the schematic, the corrector changes the purple direction to yellow; backtracking shortens the step to the green feasible update.
figures.headline: The predictor and corrector share one Cholesky factorization, and backtracking keeps the step inside the feasible bounds.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Efficient kinematics: parallel local poses feed serial world composition, while prepared contributors enable independent Jacobian columns (top). The backward pass accumulates link wrenches once, then gathers them per actuator, avoiding repeated ancestor walks (bottom).
figures.headline: Kinematics computes local poses in parallel and accumulates link wrenches once, so each actuator gathers them without repeated ancestor walks.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Collision pruning and reuse. On-the-fly link AABBs eliminate sphere–sphere tests between separated links (left). Sweep bounds prune distant obstacles; adjacent half-sweeps share the SDF at $x_{t}$ and rotate their summed gradient once (right). $m_{\pm}$ denote neighboring midpoints.
figures.headline: Collision pruning skips tests between separated links and distant obstacles, and adjacent half-sweeps share one distance evaluation.

figures.headline: Inverse dynamics runs independent chains concurrently and computes loss gradients directly, so payload updates need no recompilation.

abstract: We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated planner that reduces both planning latency and execution time for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited motions. B-spline trajectory optimization reduces the required iterations, while accelerated robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics reduce refinement cost and accommodate changing payloads. TimeOpt optimizes traversal speed along the fixed path under sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque constraints, exploiting local spline support to solve banded Newton systems efficiently on the GPU. With a 3 kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieves 4.4 ms mean planning time on RTX 5090, $14.7\times$ faster than cuRoboV2. Our method on Jetson AGX Orin plans faster than cuRoboV1 + TOPPRA on RTX 5090. A stereo-camera-based deployment on YAM achieves 5.93 s mean completed pick-and-drop cycles, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2. Code (Apache 2.0): github.com/NVlabs/curobo. Project Page: research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/curobov2-fast/.

sections.body: The section frames planning cost and execution time together, since payload changes and actuator limits can make a shorter path slower to run. It lists six contributions. B-spline trajectory optimization matches cuRoboV1 success with 25 versus 125 initial iterations. TimeOpt retimes the fixed path under velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds, reducing mean motion duration by 15.7% beyond uniform timestep refinement. A parallel GPU tree search gives 0.305 ms mean route initialization. The integrated pipeline reaches 4.4 ms mean planning time with a 3 kg payload on RTX 5090 while maintaining similar success. A stereo-camera pick-and-drop deployment on YAM reports 5.93 s mean cycle time, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Planning time and execution time both matter, and cuRoboV2-Fast targets both for payload-aware, torque-limited motions.

sections.body: The section places the work among parallel planners, B-spline trajectory optimizers, and fixed-path timing methods. VAMP uses CPU SIMD instructions, pRRTC spreads tree expansion across GPU threads, and cuRoboV1 pairs geometric initialization with parallel optimization. For timing, Bobrow et al. consider torque bounds, Verscheure et al. formulate path timing as convex optimization, and TOPPRA handles velocity, acceleration, and torque constraints. TimeOpt adopts the same fixed-path dynamics reduction but optimizes a cubic B-spline of squared speed under sampled bounds. It reports a mean latency of 0.28 ms on valid 100 g benchmark queries on RTX 5090. The paper contrasts its runtime-data approach with GRiD, which relies on robot-specific code generation.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers parallel planners, B-spline refinement, and fixed-path timing, and the method builds on each.

sections.body: The planner seeds optimization with a bounded bidirectional tree search when a straight-line seed fails. Trees grow in synchronized parallel rounds, and validation is separated from growth so checks can be added without changing growth kernels. The B-spline optimizer evaluates each sample from four controls, and its backward pass gathers gradients per control, avoiding atomic accumulation. TimeOpt optimizes a second spline of squared path speed under velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque bounds. Its primal–dual predictor–corrector solver uses banded Newton systems from the local spline support. Differentiable inverse dynamics keeps the chain schedule and inertial parameters as runtime data, so payload updates need no recompilation. Grasp planning ranks IK solutions and plans pregrasp, approach, and lift motions. The section notes that TimeOpt does not guarantee global optimality and that IK feasibility alone does not establish a collision-free path.
sections.heading: Approach
sections.headline: The planner fits B-spline trajectories to a parallel tree-search seed, then retimes them with TimeOpt under payload-dependent torque limits.

sections.body: The experiments cover route initialization, torque-limited optimization, robot computations, and pick-and-place on Franka Panda, G1, and YAM. Coarsely checked routes succeed in 98.68% of 2,575 queries, versus 91.92% for cuRoboV1 PRM, at a mean 0.305 ms. With 25 initial iterations, the B-spline formulation reaches 93% validated success against 64% for cuRoboV1. With payloads, cuRoboV2-Fast matches cuRoboV2 success and plans in 4.43 ms on RTX 5090. VAMP initializes routes faster but has lower payload success. On the real robot, mean arm execution time falls by 44.8% relative to cuRoboV2, measured over approximately 50 cycles for cuRoboV2-Fast and 15 for cuRoboV2.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Experiments show lower planning and motion times than cuRoboV2 at similar success, with real-robot gains in arm execution time.

sections.body: The discussion attributes planning-time gains to fewer optimization iterations and cheaper iterations, and it reports similar success to cuRoboV2 across payloads. It notes that shorter joint-space paths do not necessarily give shorter motions under actuator limits. TimeOpt's 15.7% reduction beyond uniform timestep refinement is presented as an opportunity for further improvement. On the real robot, more time near the velocity limit reduces arm execution time by 44.8%, while planning accounts for only 1.0% of cycle time. The stated limits are that global optimality is not guaranteed and that contact-rich manipulation, including reliable grasps, is now the main bottleneck. The paper reports a mean pick-and-transfer cycle time of 5.9 s on a real robot.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Fewer iterations, cheaper iterations, and TimeOpt timing drive the gains, while planning is only 1.0% of real-robot cycle time.
